title: Herb Scissors Cleaning Hacks for Busy Home Cooks
meta_description: Discover practical herb scissors cleaning hacks for busy home cooks. Learn how to keep your five‑blade herb shears pristine with simple, fast techniques.
html:
Keeping herb scissors clean can feel like a chore, but a few smart herb scissors cleaning hacks can turn it into a quick, almost invisible task. Whether you’re snipping cilantro for tacos or mincing basil for pesto, the five‑blade herb shears do the work in seconds—just don’t let residue turn them into a kitchen nightmare. Below are the steps I rely on after every use, plus extra tips for stubborn build‑up, so your Herb Scissors stay sharp and ready for the next chop.

Why a Dedicated Cleaning Comb Matters

The Herb Scissors come with a tiny cleaning comb designed to fit between the blades. That comb is the secret weapon for most of the hacks that follow. Without it, tiny bits of leaf and stem can hide in the gaps, eventually dulling the edges and harboring flavor‑transfer. Using the comb right after you finish chopping clears most debris before it even has a chance to dry.

Immediate Post‑Use Routine

When you’re done snipping, follow this three‑step routine. It takes less than 30 seconds and prevents the need for soaking.

  1. Shake it out. Hold the scissors over the trash can and give them a quick shake. Loose pieces fall away.
  2. Brush with the comb. Run the cleaning comb through the blades, both forward and backward. The fine teeth scrape out particles lodged between the blades.
  3. Wipe with a damp cloth. A lightly moistened paper towel or kitchen cloth removes any remaining green film. Avoid soaking the scissors; a quick wipe is enough.

After you’ve completed these steps, store the scissors in a dry drawer or hang them on a magnetic strip. The less moisture they see, the longer the blades stay rust‑free.

Deep‑Clean Hack for Sticky Herbs

If you’re working with particularly oily herbs—think basil with a splash of olive oil or cilantro in a soupy sauce—residue can cling to the blades. Here’s a safe deep‑clean method that won’t blunt the edges.

  • Fill a bowl with warm, soapy water. Use a few drops of mild dish soap; avoid harsh detergents that can corrode steel.
  • Submerge only the blades. Hold the handles and dip the cutting edge for 20–30 seconds. The warm water loosens stuck particles.
  • Use the comb while submerged. Gently run the cleaning comb through the blades under water. The soap acts as a lubricant, making it easier to dislodge stubborn bits.
  • Rinse and dry immediately. A quick rinse under running water removes soap, then pat the blades dry with a microfiber cloth. Don’t let the scissors air‑dry, as that can cause water spots.

This hack is quick enough to fit into a busy cooking schedule, yet thorough enough to keep your Herb Scissors performing like new.

Preventive Care: Keeping Build‑Up at Bay

Even with regular cleaning, some herbs leave a faint green film that can accumulate over weeks. A preventive tip is to lightly coat the blades with food‑grade mineral oil once a month. The oil creates a barrier that reduces adhesion, making each subsequent cleaning easier.

To apply, drizzle a few drops of mineral oil onto a soft cloth and rub it onto the blades, avoiding the pivot point. Wipe off any excess with a clean cloth. The oil won’t affect the taste of your herbs, and it adds a subtle shine that signals a well‑maintained tool.

When to Replace Your Herb Scissors

All kitchen tools have a lifespan. If you notice the blades no longer cut cleanly, or if the comb no longer reaches into the gaps, it’s time to consider a replacement. The five‑blade design is engineered for precision, and a dull set can damage delicate herbs, turning them mushy instead of finely minced. Investing in a new pair ensures you keep the same speed and consistency you rely on for quick prep.

FAQ

Can I put my herb scissors in the dishwasher?

It’s best to avoid the dishwasher. The high heat and harsh detergents can dull the blades and damage the small cleaning comb. Hand‑washing with the methods above preserves sharpness.

Is the cleaning comb safe for stainless‑steel blades?

Yes. The comb is made from food‑grade plastic with gentle teeth that won’t scratch stainless steel. It’s specifically designed for the Herb Scissors' five‑blade configuration.

How often should I oil the blades?

Apply a thin coat of food‑grade mineral oil about once a month, or whenever you notice a slight green film building up after several uses. This preventive step keeps the blades slick and eases cleaning.
